children.author: luiwammus
children.text: The original result from 2010 implied that the paths were longer by a small linear factor (I believe 1.05n), so many people still held out hope that efficient simplex algorithms could exist that would take e.g. 2n steps. This result completely kills such hope as it shows that there is a family that has super-polynomial (in n) diameter . So it is much more than a 'mopping up' result, it was one of the biggest open questions in Optimization, and has a big impact on the community.

children.author: akoboldfrying
children.text:
Maybe it's in the article, which I haven't read, but: Are we certain that we can't start simplex from a sufficiently-close-to-optimal vertex? Because if we can, poly-time simplex would not be ruled out.

(I was about to follow that with: There might be easy tricks available here -- e.g., if we can upper-bound the number or fraction of superpolynomial-length paths in any polytope to some polynomial function f(nVars, nConstraints), it would suffice to interleave f(nVars, nConstraints)+1 simplex runs, each starting from a different point. But I realised that no such polynomial upper bound could exist, since even 1 long path necessarily already contains a superpolynomial number of subpaths that are themselves long.)

For context, this means that there is no polynomial-time simplex algorithm (which is an algorithm for linear programming (optimization)). The original version of the conjecture was an attempt to explain why the simplex method seemed to work surprisingly well in practice, but it was disproved in 2010 (after 50+ years!). This seems like more of a mopping up result.

children.author: mattalex
children.text:
I cannot talk about gurobi specifically, but that's not an uncommon approach for pure LPs and root MIP relaxations.

Simplex is pretty single threaded since you perform many sequential pivots. If you want to parallelize you basically have to use things like parallel pricing. This is of course also true for interior point, but the difference is that interior point uses fewer, larger steps, which work more nicely on parallel hw.

for milp this is less useful since you want a basic solution and warm start is much better done with a dual simplex.

There are still some big things you can do for simplex, e.g. we get closer and closer to block pivots becoming viable.
I'm not really an LP person anymore, but I remember Gurobi using a mixture of Simplex and interior point pretty heavily? Might just be if you have a bunch of spare cores though.

Most general convex solvers used in production are interior point solvers.

For LPs, simplex frequently ends up better because it is naturally well conditioned (you don't need e.g. LU factors), and because solutions are basic you can use row generation to add in constraints as they become relevant.

The latter is particularly helpful for combinatorial optimization or when iteratively refining linearizations of convex problems.

Interior point for LPs become interesting when your problem is somewhat degenerate. In well structured problems one can exploit the polytope surface to quickly step through bases without needing to factorize or even materialize large matrices
Someone correct if I'm mistaken, but I understand interior point methods are also used for quadratic programming, for example as used by SpaceX in their landing algorithms.

children.author: angry_octet
children.text: Simplex often has very fast solves but WCET is exponential. Interior point methods can achieve polynomial time, but have a much larger cost for setup and can be expensive for each step. Simplex problems with new constraints can often start at a previous solution and slide along the solution face quickly.

Extra info:

In real-world logistics, the shapes are generally nice and convex, not "adversarially warped", so Simplex is fast.

Apparently when guaranteed polynomial speed is needed, solvers use interior-point methods, which tunnel straight through the inside of the shape rather than walking along the outside edges, which is unaffected by the new result anyway.

children.author: Lapalux
children.text: thank you!

I always like to try to translate it to a really simple English version:

You can represent many problems like logistics with a list of linear requirements so valid combinations form a multi-dimensional geometric shape where every corner of that shape and inside that shape represents a 'valid' but probably not optimal solution, e.g. every package gets delivered by a driver, but not the lowest fuel or time, and 'valid' so no rules are broken, like no driver is scheduled more than >24 hours in one day.

Every edge is a single step that changes one variable. It's interesting and useful because surprisingly the representation means the optimal solution will always lie on an outside corner. You generally start somewhere 'warm' and try to get hotter, that's the Simplex algorithm.

The polynomial Hirsch conjecture was that the number of steps between any two corners grows polynomially as you add more variables and rules, limiting how many steps you might need to find that optimal corner. Now we know you need more steps.

Hope I saved you time/tokens though.

children.author: tensegrist
akoboldfrying
children.text: Nice explanation, thanks.

think of a cube as a graph: how many edges do you need to get from one vertex to another, in the worst case?

we can ask this question more generally for "polytopes" — graphs that generalize the notions of polygons and polyhedra

the original hirsch conjecture said for an n-faced polytope of dimension d you do not require any more than n-d steps to get from any vertex to any other, which is false

the polynomial hirsch conjecture relaxes this to the existence of some constant k for which the bound is O(n^k)
